# Automatically marshal cancellation arguments in JSInterop

<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request to our repo. -->

<!-- If this is your first PR in the ASP.NET Core repo, please run through the checklist
below to ensure a smooth review and merge process for your PR. -->

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

<!-- Once all that is done, you're ready to go. Open the PR with the content below. -->

Automatically project raw AbortSignal and CancellationToken arguments.

## Description

**Revised to the user-confirmed application API: raw values, no reference factory or wrapper.** This supersedes both previous drafts. Specification and full consumer examples: #70326. API/convention proposal: #70327. Implementation: dcd2191693. The PR remains experimental and DRAFT; user confirmation of the examples is not API-review approval.

### Exact application-facing shape

JS to .NET instance method:

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const pending = dotnetObject.invokeMethodAsync("Yolo", controller.signal);
controller.abort();
const result = await pending;
```

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public Task<string> Yolo(CancellationToken cancellationToken);
```

JS to .NET static method, without an application DotNetObjectReference:

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const pending = DotNet.invokeMethodAsync("MyApp", "YoloStatic", controller.signal);
controller.abort();
const result = await pending;
```

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public static Task<string> YoloStatic(CancellationToken cancellationToken);
```

.NET to JavaScript:

```csharp
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
var pending = jsRuntime.InvokeAsync<string>("yolo", args: [cts.Token]);
cts.Cancel();
var result = await pending;
```

```javascript
globalThis.yolo = async function (signal) {
    const response = await fetch("/data", { signal });
    return await response.text();
};
```

`args: [cts.Token]` deliberately supplies an ordinary argument, not the separate invocation-control token. JavaScript receives a native AbortSignal. No application factory, wrapper constructor, initialization await or bridge disposal is required. Tokens can occur in any parameter position and in supported argument objects.

### What changed

- Remove `createCancellationTokenReference`, `DotNetCancellationTokenReference.CreateAsync`, explicit cancellation owners, and all prior invocation-cancellation APIs/protocol. Keep ordinary invocation signatures and promise outcomes.
- Recognize raw signals in the normal JS async argument path and prepare internal references with the call's existing dispatcher, including static calls. Share in-flight initialization and live bridges for concurrent/repeated signals.
- Snapshot application serialization once, recording signal locations. After setup, edit only those locations in the data-only snapshot. Preserve getters/toJSON exactly once and byte-array values; flush bytes immediately before the final application invocation, after any intermediate setup calls.
- Marshal raw .NET token arguments through an internal descriptor. None/pre-canceled tokens need no live bridge; live serialized occurrences get independent observer references so one released ID cannot invalidate later queued metadata. The JS reviver supplies native signals.
- Own resources in the runtimes. Abort/notification completes links; WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry also release abandoned, never-canceled signals. Argument leases protect in-flight consumers. Managed runtime disposal releases remaining automatic references. Cleanup never requests cancellation or disposes caller-owned sources/controllers.
- Preserve retained values after call return and normal results from handlers that ignore/catch cancellation. Pre-aborted input still invokes .NET with a canceled token. Generic `createJSObjectReference(signal)` values retain their generic reference meaning.
- Roll back new observers on serialization AND synchronous dispatch failure, while preserving successfully dispatched nested calls. Remove the manual-owner public API baseline entries; the remaining framework callback surface is listed for API review.

### Validation

Final runs on Windows/Chromium: **187 managed tests passed** (17 new automatic/reference cases and every Boolean row inspected), and **32 browser tests passed**: 15 shared cases plus one existing ordinary-interop control in EACH of Server and WebAssembly. Both runtime cells were observed independently.

Coverage includes both raw mappings; static calls with both pre-cancel rows; real managed cancellation with normal handler results; ignored cancellation; independent/reused/concurrent signals; token/native signal retention after call return; native pre-canceled fetch; unchanged control-token behavior and generic JS object references; getter/toJSON once; byte-array snapshots; serialization/dispatch rollback; and incoming/outgoing GC cleanup.

The GC cases drive ACTUAL Chrome collection using HeapProfiler.collectGarbage, not direct finalizer invocation. They observe the actual managed automatic-reference count return to zero without requesting cancellation. This closes the retention issue of keeping every successful call's bridge until runtime end.

Exact commands, from the worktree root (`. .\activate.ps1` before dotnet; tests used `ASPNETCORE_TEST_LOG_MAXPATH=32767`):

```powershell
# Passed: standalone package declarations
node_modules\.bin\tsc.cmd --build src\Components\Web.JS\JSInterop\tsconfig.json --pretty false

# Passed: no lint errors
node_modules\.bin\eslint.cmd -c src\Components\Web.JS\src\.eslintrc.js src\Components\Web.JS\src\JSInterop\Microsoft.JSInterop.ts --quiet

# Passed: Debug and Release browser bundles
Push-Location src\Components\Web.JS; npm run build; Pop-Location

# Passed: 187 tests
dotnet test src\Components\JSInterop\test\Microsoft.JSInterop.Tests.csproj --no-restore -v:q -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:GenerateInstallers=false --logger 'console;verbosity=normal'

# Passed: 0 warnings, 0 errors
dotnet build src\Components\test\E2ETest\Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests.csproj --no-restore -v:q -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:GenerateInstallers=false

# Passed: 32 tests, 16 per runtime
dotnet test src\Components\test\E2ETest\Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests.csproj --no-build --no-restore -v:q -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:GenerateInstallers=false --filter 'FullyQualifiedName~InteropCancellationTest|FullyQualifiedName~InteropTest.CanInvokeInteropMethods' --logger 'console;verbosity=normal'
```

**Negative controls:** disable incoming source cancellation and report false for outgoing cancellation. Two managed producer assertions fail. Server browser final assertions fail with expected `canceled in .NET`/actual `running`, and expected `aborted in JS`/actual `native signal retained`. All four static controls (two rows in each runtime) stay green. Restored source passes all final suites. Raw-revision negative browser checks were on Server; WebAssembly has full positive coverage, not an additional claimed negative run.

A canonical per-page Server sample first proved instance/static raw inputs and a raw C# token producing a native signal, with no observed errors/failed resources in the final probe. Removed after permanent coverage passed; servers stopped.

### Review and remaining boundaries

Architecture and full fresh-context correctness/test-validity reviews completed. The latter found a real leak when BeginInvokeJS throws after serialization. The observer rollback scope now extends through dispatch. The focused regression proved one observer existed at the throwing producer, failed expected0/actual1 without cleanup, then passed with cleanup. A fresh follow-up confirmed the finding resolved; the final187+32 suites were repeated green after that correction.

Still experimental: public marshalling convention and framework callback placement; browser WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry prerequisites; nondeterministic GC timing; allocations and extra snapshot traversal; pending observation impact on circuit activity/pause; and host-specific teardown/disconnection cleanup. Live uncanceled values can retain resources while observable. Async notification/cleanup failures are logged explicitly, not used as a new invocation outcome. No benchmark or deterministic GC deadline is claimed.

WebView, Native AOT/trimming publish, multithreaded WebAssembly, actual mixed-runtime E2E, Auto transitions, reconnect/resume, non-Chromium and remote cleanup after transport/runtime teardown remain unverified. Static SSR/prerender have no JS interop. Managed teardown cleanup is implemented; comprehensive remote cleanup is not claimed. Installer validation is not claimed.

Keep this PR **draft**. No API approval, ready state, merge or auto-merge is requested. No AI.Mcp changes or dependency are included.

Relates to #70326.

## Bug Description
Blazor Server transfers files selected through InputFile from the browser to the server as chunked JS data streams.

The problem appears when several large files are opened and placed in a multipart HTTP request:

- A separate remote stream starts for each browser file.
- The multipart request consumes those streams sequentially.
- Streams that are not currently being consumed can continue sending and eventually fill their server-side pipe.
- The previous implementation awaited pipe backpressure while running on the circuit dispatcher.
- Once one unconsumed stream blocked that dispatcher, chunks for the stream currently being consumed could no longer be processed.

Neither stream could make progress, so the HTTP request hung and never reached the target API action.
Increasing SignalR message size, stream buffer capacity, or HTTP request-body limits does not address this deadlock because it originates in coordination between the circuit dispatcher, the pipe writer, and multiple concurrent browser-file streams.

## Description of code changes

- Fixed Blazor Server multiple-file uploads hanging under pipe backpressure. 
- The server now rejects chunks temporarily instead of blocking the circuit, while JavaScript retries the same chunk with exponential backoff. 
- Added managed and JavaScript tests for backpressure, retries, stream disposal, timeout handling, and per-chunk acknowledgements.

## Test changes
RemoteJSDataStreamTest.cs updates existing Boolean assertions to use the new result enum and adds coverage proving that:

- A full pipe rejects additional chunks rather than blocking.
- The rejected chunk can be retried successfully after buffered data is consumed.
- Backpressure retries refresh activity and do not incorrectly trigger the stream timeout.

CircuitStreamingInterop.test.ts adds coverage proving that:

- Every chunk is acknowledged.
- A rejected chunk is retried without advancing its position or ID.
- Sending stops when the stream is disposed.
- Completion still occurs if error reporting fails after the connection closes.

After

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8d7fdc7f-88df-45cd-b2a9-9d4f34eeaa5f


Fixes #47301

## Summary

Propose automatic, bidirectional marshalling of raw AbortSignal and CancellationToken argument values through existing JSInterop invocation APIs. Application code passes the value itself; the runtimes establish and own the internal reference bridge. There is no application reference factory, wrapper constructor, initialization await or bridge-disposal step.

Cancellation remains a parameter value, not an invocation mode. This replaces both earlier drafts: call-level invocation cancellation and manually created cancellation references. The examples below were explicitly confirmed by the user; that confirmation is not API-review approval.

## Motivation and goals

1. Support `dotnetObject.invokeMethodAsync("Yolo", abortSignal)` with a CancellationToken parameter, without an additional creation step.
2. Support static calls such as `DotNet.invokeMethodAsync("MyApp", "YoloStatic", abortSignal)` without an application DotNetObjectReference.
3. Support `jsRuntime.InvokeAsync<string>("yolo", args: [cancellationToken])`, with JavaScript receiving a native AbortSignal automatically.
4. Preserve ordinary invocation results/errors, receiver-controlled cooperative cancellation, and value lifetimes beyond one call.
5. Own setup, sharing, cleanup, serialization snapshots and failure rollback inside the runtimes.

## In scope

- Raw AbortSignal arguments on ordinary instance AND static JS-to-.NET calls.
- Raw CancellationToken values in C# args arrays, received as native AbortSignal values.
- No application factory, wrapper constructor, initialization await or bridge disposal.
- Retention/reuse, pre-cancel, independent/shared/concurrent signals, serialization snapshots, automatic notification/GC cleanup and failure rollback.

## Out of scope

1. Automatically cancel an invocation, reject its promise, skip a method for pre-canceled input or undo work.
2. Reinterpret the existing InvokeAsync invocation-control token as an argument.
3. Require callers to create/dispose interop references, or translate arbitrary JavaScript abort reasons into .NET exceptions.
4. Infer that a cancellation value is unused merely because its supplying call returned or failed.
5. Claim complete coverage of WebView, Native AOT/trimming publish, multithreaded WebAssembly, actual mixed runtimes, Auto transitions, reconnect/resume or non-Chromium browsers.

## Risks / unknowns

This supersedes both previous drafts. User confirmation of the literal examples is not API approval. Raw marshalling is a new public behavior and framework callback placement remains provisional. WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry are browser prerequisites and collection is nondeterministic. Live uncanceled values retain observer/reference resources; observation can affect circuit activity/pause and needs further lifecycle analysis. No benchmark is claimed. WebView, Native AOT/trimming publish, multithreaded WebAssembly, actual mixed runtimes, Auto transitions, reconnect/resume, non-Chromium and remote cleanup after transport/runtime teardown are unverified. Static calls retain their existing default-dispatcher requirements.

## Examples

Normal asynchronous interop recognizes raw AbortSignal and CancellationToken values in ordinary arguments and prepares the projection internally. Tokens can occupy any parameter position and occur in serialized objects. The instance call uses its existing dispatcher; the static API retains its existing default-runtime selection rules.

### JS to .NET instance method

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const pending = dotnetObject.invokeMethodAsync("Yolo", controller.signal);
controller.abort();
const result = await pending;
```

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public Task<string> Yolo(CancellationToken cancellationToken);
```

These are application signatures/calls; the method's own body decides how to use the token. No caller-created cancellation reference appears.

### JS to .NET static method

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const pending = DotNet.invokeMethodAsync("MyApp", "YoloStatic", controller.signal);
controller.abort();
const result = await pending;
```

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public static Task<string> YoloStatic(CancellationToken cancellationToken);
```

No application object reference is needed. The internal infrastructure can still use reference-backed callbacks to implement the mapping.

### .NET to JavaScript

```csharp
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
var pending = jsRuntime.InvokeAsync<string>("yolo", args: [cts.Token]);
cts.Cancel();
var result = await pending;
```

```javascript
globalThis.yolo = async function (signal) {
    const response = await fetch("/data", { signal });
    return await response.text();
};
```

JavaScript receives a native AbortSignal suitable for browser APIs. The original source/controller belongs to application code; only the internal bridge belongs to interop.

### Invocation control token is distinct

The `args: [cts.Token]` spelling is deliberate. The existing CancellationToken overload parameter controls only the managed interop wait. Canceling that control token does not abort a separately supplied signal argument or stop a JavaScript function that ignores it.

### Pre-cancel, normal failure and ignored cancellation

A pre-aborted input still invokes the .NET method with an already-canceled token. A pre-canceled .NET token produces an already-aborted native signal before entering JavaScript; fetch then applies fetch's own cancellation behavior. CancellationToken.None produces a non-aborted signal without a live observer.

A handler can ignore the token and complete normally, or catch cancellation and return a normal result. Normal handler exceptions remain normal interop errors. There is no new framework promise-settlement policy.

### Retained values, repeated use and concurrency

A receiver can retain a token or signal after returning and observe later cancellation. Repeated/concurrent uses of the same JavaScript signal in a runtime share its bridge and its initialization, without duplicate listeners. Signal reuse after cancellation remains valid and supplies a canceled token.

Each serialized live .NET token occurrence can produce a distinct native signal observing the same original token. Native signal identity across occurrences is not promised; cancellation behavior is shared. Independent input sources remain independent.

### Automatic cleanup

Cancellation completion releases the no-longer-needed internal links, coordinated with in-flight argument uses. Browser collection of an unreachable signal also releases its bridge through WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry without requesting cancellation. Collection is nondeterministic; there is no caller disposal obligation or deterministic reclamation deadline.

Live uncanceled signals can retain their registrations/references while still observable. Managed runtime disposal releases remaining automatic managed references. Remote/browser cleanup after transport loss or runtime teardown remains a separate unverified host/lifecycle boundary.

Retained .NET tokens remain valid after reference release, including late registration against a canceled token. Cleaning up the bridge does not dispose caller-owned sources or force application cancellation.

### Serialization and setup failures

Application getters and toJSON execute once. Argument values, including byte arrays, are snapshotted before asynchronous signal setup; byte-array transfer occurs immediately before the final application invocation so intermediate bridge calls cannot consume the wrong batch.

Setup failure rejects the invocation through its normal failure path, releases all acquired preparation leases, and does not invalidate a previously used shared projection. .NET serialization failure rolls back new observers for that serialization, including reentrant serialization cases. Generic createJSObjectReference(signal) arguments remain generic IJSObjectReference values, preserving their existing meaning.

Async notification/cleanup errors are reported explicitly to the browser console rather than silently changing the application invocation's outcome.

## Assumptions

- The browser supports AbortSignal, AbortController, WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry; no polyfill is introduced.
- Receivers cooperate if they want cancellation. Projection cannot interrupt arbitrary work.
- Async interop is available and the framework assets are from one build. SSR/prerender have no JS interop.
- Static calls retain existing default-dispatcher requirements; object calls retain runtime affinity.
- GC-driven cleanup is eventual, not a replacement for application ownership of its own CTS/controller.
- Public marshalling behavior and framework callback surface require API review. User confirmation of the examples is not API approval.

## Experiment and validation

This replaces the manual reference-factory experiment in the same DRAFT PR #70328. Separate API/convention review remains #70327. The concrete instance, static and C# examples above are the agreed application surface; none requires a caller-owned interop bridge. Framework callback plumbing in PublicAPI.Unshipped does not constitute API approval.

Internally, JavaScript serializes application values once and records raw-signal locations, defers byte-array transmission until setup completes, and substitutes internal reference metadata into the data-only snapshot. Per-dispatcher initialization is shared by repeated/concurrent signals. Argument leases protect in-flight consumers. .NET raw-token serialization creates an internal observer only for a live token; the JS reviver supplies a native signal. Weak signal ownership and real FinalizationRegistry cleanup reclaim abandoned projections, not just canceled ones. Runtime disposal clears remaining automatic managed references. No new operation-cancellation mode, forced promise settlement, or final-token injection is present.

You may find the [Framework Design Guidelines](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/coding-guidelines/framework-design-guidelines-digest.md) helpful.
-->

No new application invocation method, factory, reference type or JS wrapper is required. Existing signatures remain:

```typescript
DotNetObject.invokeMethodAsync<T>(methodIdentifier: string, ...args: any[]): Promise<T>;
DotNet.invokeMethodAsync<T>(assemblyName: string, methodIdentifier: string, ...args: any[]): Promise<T>;
```

```csharp
ValueTask<TValue> IJSRuntime.InvokeAsync<TValue>(string identifier, object?[]? args);
ValueTask<TValue> IJSRuntime.InvokeAsync<TValue>(
    string identifier, CancellationToken cancellationToken, object?[]? args);
```

**New public marshalling convention:** a raw JavaScript AbortSignal argument maps automatically to a normal .NET CancellationToken parameter, in any position or inside supported argument objects. A raw CancellationToken argument maps automatically to a native JavaScript AbortSignal. It is not the separate invocation-control token. Pre-aborted input still invokes .NET; there is no special promise cancellation outcome.

The earlier `createCancellationTokenReference`, `DotNetCancellationTokenReference.CreateAsync`, explicit owners and `invokeMethodAsyncWithCancellation` APIs are removed from the draft. There are no new application-facing JavaScript exports.

The current prototype retains this public framework callback plumbing because existing static JSInvokable discovery uses exported types. It is not a consumer factory and needs API review/placement discussion. This is the complete new .NET surface against main, recorded in PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt:

```diff
 namespace Microsoft.JSInterop
 {
+    public sealed class JSCancellationTokenReference : System.IAsyncDisposable
+    {
+        public System.Threading.CancellationToken Token { get; }
+        [JSInvokable("CreateCancellationTokenReference")]
+        public static DotNetObjectReference<JSCancellationTokenReference> Create(
+            IJSObjectReference signal, bool isAborted);
+        [JSInvokable]
+        public System.Threading.Tasks.Task CancelAsync();
+        [JSInvokable]
+        public System.Threading.Tasks.ValueTask DisposeAsync();
+    }
 }
```

No constructor is public. Framework-only callback naming/placement is provisional; applications write none of these calls.

## Usage Examples

<!--
Please provide code examples that highlight how the proposed API additions are meant to be consumed.
This will help suggest whether the API has the right shape to be functional, performant and useable.
You can use code blocks like this:
```csharp
// some lines of code here
```
-->

### JS to .NET instance method

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const pending = dotnetObject.invokeMethodAsync("Yolo", controller.signal);
controller.abort();
const result = await pending;
```

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public Task<string> Yolo(CancellationToken cancellationToken);
```

### JS to .NET static method

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const pending = DotNet.invokeMethodAsync("MyApp", "YoloStatic", controller.signal);
controller.abort();
const result = await pending;
```

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public static Task<string> YoloStatic(CancellationToken cancellationToken);
```

No application DotNetObjectReference is needed for the static call. Static runtime selection follows the existing API.

### .NET to JavaScript

```csharp
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
var pending = jsRuntime.InvokeAsync<string>("yolo", args: [cts.Token]);
cts.Cancel();
var result = await pending;
```

```javascript
globalThis.yolo = async function (signal) {
    const response = await fetch("/data", { signal });
    return await response.text();
};
```

`args: [cts.Token]` is intentional: it supplies an ordinary argument. Passing a CancellationToken as the overload's control parameter still cancels only the managed wait. Both token/signal values can remain live after a call returns, with no user-created or user-disposed bridge.

## Alternative Designs

<!--
Were there other options you considered, such as alternative API shapes?
How does this compare to analogous APIs in other ecosystems and libraries?
-->

- Call-ID cancellation, final-token injection and special invocation methods: the wrong abstraction; removed.
- Explicit async reference factories/owners: rejected by the user in favor of automatic raw arguments; removed.
- Hidden asynchronous work inside a synchronous converter: instead the JS async invocation pipeline prepares signal references, and the .NET token converter emits a descriptor consumed by the JS reviver.
- Cleanup on call completion: would break retained values. Notification, browser GC and runtime teardown own cleanup instead.
- Retain every successful call's bridge until runtime end: avoid this with weak signal ownership and real FinalizationRegistry cleanup.
- Global-only signal setup: instance calls use their existing dispatcher; static calls use the existing static dispatcher. No extra application object is needed.
- Re-serialize application objects after an await: would rerun getters/toJSON and break byte-array staging. The implementation snapshots once, records signal locations, then edits the data-only snapshot after setup.

## Risks

<!--
Please mention any risks that to your knowledge the API proposal might entail, such as breaking changes, performance regressions, etc.
-->

- This is a new public marshalling behavior despite unchanged application method signatures. It and the framework callback surface require API review. PublicAPI.Unshipped does not confer approval.
- WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry are browser prerequisites. GC cleanup is eventual/nondeterministic. Live uncanceled values retain bridge resources until notification, collection or runtime teardown; no deterministic reclamation deadline is promised.
- An outgoing observation is an ordinary pending interop promise until cancellation/collection/teardown. Impact on circuit pause/resume and other lifecycle policies requires separate validation.
- Incoming repeated/concurrent uses share a bridge by signal identity in a runtime. Outgoing token occurrences can have distinct native signal identities; they observe the same original token. This avoids shared-ID revocation races with in-flight payloads.
- Async preparation and snapshot copying introduce allocations/round trips; large mixed payloads require an extra data-only JSON traversal. No benchmark is claimed.
- Setup failures use normal invocation failure handling. Notification/cleanup failures are logged explicitly rather than imposing a new invocation outcome.
- Generic createJSObjectReference(signal) arguments retain their generic reference meaning. Only raw signal arguments get this automatic projection.
- Server/WebAssembly and Chromium GC are validated separately. WebView, Native AOT/trimming publish, multithreaded WebAssembly, actual mixed-runtime E2E, Auto transitions, reconnect/resume and non-Chromium remain unverified. Managed runtime cleanup is implemented; comprehensive remote cleanup after disconnection remains an unverified boundary.

### Source justifications

```text
Raw API: "dotnetObject.invokeMethodAsync(\"Yolo\", abortSignal) should be what the user writes. Equivalent on the c# side" — user clarification captured in revised #70326
Static calls: "And obviously should also work with \"static methods\" without requiring a dotnet reference" — user clarification captured in revised #70326
Automatic values: "Application code does not create, wrap, or dispose interop cancellation references." — implementation README
No forced promise result: "Abort signals cancel the token, not the interop promise" — implementation README
Getter/byte preservation: "Application getters and toJSON execute once" — revised specification and real-browser snapshot test
Actual callback surface: declarations above match PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt and JSCancellationTokenReference.cs in [dcd2191693](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/commit/dcd2191693211df7eef0d3a9beeae15eab9f704e)
Cleanup: "Collection is nondeterministic and does not request cancellation." — implementation README and both-runtime GC tests using Chrome HeapProfiler.collectGarbage
Control-token distinction: "The separate invocation-control token still cancels only the managed wait" — implementation README and both-runtime control-token test
```

Full validation commands, red/green evidence and runtime boundaries are on #70326 and draft #70328. This revision replaces the prior proposal rather than asserting approval of it.

## Summary

This PR improves the developer experience when JavaScript interop calls timeout in Blazor applications by throwing a descriptive `TimeoutException` instead of a generic `TaskCanceledException`.

## Problem

When JavaScript interop calls timeout (through `JSRuntime.DefaultAsyncTimeout`), developers receive a generic `TaskCanceledException` that does not indicate the timeout was the cause. This makes debugging timeout issues difficult.

Before:
```csharp
await JSRuntime.InvokeAsync<string>("longRunningFunction");
// Throws: TaskCanceledException — unclear what caused the cancellation
```

After:
```csharp
await JSRuntime.InvokeAsync<string>("longRunningFunction");
// Throws: TimeoutException("The JS interop call 'longRunningFunction' timed out after 00:01:00.")
```

## Root Cause

`JSRuntime.InvokeAsync` creates a `CancellationTokenSource` with `DefaultAsyncTimeout` and passes its token to the inner invoke method. When the timeout fires, the CTS cancels the token, which sets the `TaskCompletionSource` to canceled. The resulting `TaskCanceledException` is indistinguishable from user-initiated cancellation.

## Changes

### `JSRuntime.cs`
- Wrapped the timeout-path `await` in a try/catch that catches `OperationCanceledException` when the timeout CTS has fired (`cts.IsCancellationRequested`)
- Re-throws as `TimeoutException` with a descriptive message including the JS identifier and timeout duration

### `JSRuntimeTest.cs`
- Updated `InvokeAsync_ThrowsTimeoutException_AfterDefaultTimeout` to expect `TimeoutException` and verify the message contains the identifier
- Added `InvokeAsync_CancelsWithTaskCanceledException_WhenCancellationTokenFiresBeforeTimeout` to verify explicit `CancellationToken` still throws `TaskCanceledException`

## Multi-Model Exploration

| Model | Approach | Verdict |
|-------|----------|---------|
| claude-opus-4.6-fast | Catch OCE in JSRuntime, throw TimeoutException | ✅ Selected — minimal, correct |
| claude-sonnet-4.6 | Analyzed 4 alternatives (TCS fault, ComponentBase, AsyncLocal, etc.) | All worse than selected |
| gpt-5.1-codex | Analyzed 3 alternatives | Confirmed selected approach is best |

## Backward Compatibility

✅ **No breaking changes** — Only the specific `DefaultAsyncTimeout` timeout scenario changes exception type. All other cancellation behaviors remain unchanged. `ComponentBase` naturally propagates `TimeoutException` because it only swallows exceptions when `task.IsCanceled` is `true`, and `TimeoutException` produces a faulted task.

Fixes #21384.

This PR improves the developer experience when JavaScript interop calls timeout in Blazor applications by throwing a more meaningful `TimeoutException` instead of a generic `TaskCanceledException`.


## Problem

Currently, when JavaScript interop calls timeout (either through `JSRuntime.DefaultAsyncTimeout` or explicit timeout parameters, developers receive a generic `TaskCanceledException` that doesn't clearly indicate the timeout was the cause of the cancellation. ```csharp
// When a JS interop call times out, only a TaskCanceledException is thrown
await JSRuntime.InvokeAsync<string>("longRunningFunction");

```csharp

await JSRuntime.InvokeAsync<string>("longRunningFunction");
// Throws: TimeoutException with descriptive message
```

### 1. `JSRuntime` timeout detection
- Enhanced timeout handling in `JSRuntime.InvokeAsync` methods to detect when cancellation is specifically due to timeout rather than other cancellation sources.

### 2. `TimeoutException` usage
- When a timeout occurs, throw `TimeoutException` instead of allowing `TaskCanceledException` to propagate, providing developers with clear indication of what went wrong.

### 3. `ComponentBase` exception handling
- Updated `ComponentBase.CallStateHasChangedOnAsyncCompletion` to allow `TimeoutException` to propagate to user code while maintaining existing behavior for other cancelled tasks.

### 4. Test updates
- Updated relevant tests to expect `TimeoutException` for timeout scenarios while preserving existing behavior for other cancellation types.

## Backward Compatibility

✅ **No breaking changes**
-   This change only affects the specific timeout scenario, improving the exception type from a generic cancellation to a more specific timeout indication. All other cancellation behaviors remain unchanged.


Fixes #21384.

items.title: Add framework support for lazy-loading assemblies on route change

labels.name: area-blazor
labels.description: Includes: Blazor, Razor Components

labels.name: feature-blazor-wasm
labels.description: This issue is related to and / or impacts Blazor WebAssembly

items.body:
This PR adds support for lazy loading assemblies to the Blazor framework.

In some scenarios, users might want to load assemblies dynamically at runtime based on certain constraints. For example, only load the assemblies needed to render the admin sales page if the user navigates to `mysite.com/admin/sales`.

This feature is particularly helpful for users operating in the WebAssembly hosting model with pages that require a large amount of assemblies. In this case, a user can conserve network calls and local resources by not loading the assemblies they do not need.

**Note:** This feature is not useful in the Server hosting model and won't do anything useful there. If you're running in a Server hosting model, you don't have the same concerns about conserving network requests and local resources.

A user starts using this functionality by labelling the assemblies that should be lazy loaded in their project file. Like so:

```
<ItemGroup>
  <BlazorWebAssemblyLazyLoad Include="Newtonsoft.Json.dll" />
  <BlazorWebAssemblyLazyLoad Include="MegaBig.dll" />
</ItemGroup>
```

At build time, these dependencies will be marked as lazy loaded. This will prevent them from being automatically loaded at app launch time by our startup logic.

**Note:** Only assemblies that are explicitly referenced from your app can be lazy loaded. If an assembly is not referenced in the app, it won't be lazily-loaded. In fact, it won't even be part of the published output as it will be stripped by the linker.

Once a user has designated the assemblies that should be lazily-loaded, they'll need to write some code to say when they should be loaded. Enter, this PR.

The user starts by adding a `OnNavigateAsync` callback to a router component in their page.

```
<Router Assembly="typeof(App)" AdditionalAssemblies="@lazyLoadedAssemblies" OnNavigateAsync="NavigateHandler">
...
</Router>
```

The `OnNavigateAsync` handler is a callback that gets invoked whenever the user:

- Visits a route for the first time
- Navigates from one route to another

This callback provides a `NavigationContext` parameter and expects a `Task` in return.

```
public EventCallback<NavigationContext> OnNavigateAsync();
```

The `NavigationContext` object is a sealed class that exposes the following properties:

```
public sealed class NavigationContext {
  string Path;
  CancellationToken CancellationToken;
}
```

The `Path` property is the route a user is navigating to, such as `/blog/post/1` and the `CancellationToken` can be used to observe the cancellation of the async task.

**Note:** `OnNavigateAsync` automatically cancels the currently running navigation task when the user navigates away from a page.

Inside `OnNavigateAsync`, the user can implement whatever logic is needed to determine what assemblies should be loaded. Options include:

- if statements inside the `OnNavigateAsync`
- a lookup table that maps routes to assembly names that is injected into the application
- a lookup table that is implemented within the `@code` fragment

This is an implementation detail that is left to the user based on their particular scenarios.

Once I've figured out what assemblies I need to load when a user navigates to a certain `NavigationContext.Path` I need to load them.

Enter `LazyAssemblyLoader`.

`LazyAssemblyLoader` is a singleton registered in the DI. To use it, a user can inject the dependency into their page.

```
@inject LazyAssemblyLoader lazyLoader
```

The `LazyAssemblyLoader` provides a single public API method `LoadAssembliesAsync` which has the following API interface.

```
public async Task<IEnumerable<Assembly>> LoadAssembliesAsync(IEnumerable<string> assembliesToLoad)
```

Assembly names in, assemblies out. Under the hood, this method makes some JS interop calls to fetch the assemblies via a network call and load them into the runtime running on WASM.

**Note:** The implementation is designed to support pre-rendering scenarios. When pre-rendering, there is no JS runtime available to interop with. In those scenarios, we're running on the server and can assume that all assemblies are already loaded (see note above about why lazy loading on the server doesn't make sense).

So now, my Router looks something like this.

```
@inject LazyAssemblyLoader lazyLoader

<Router Assembly="typeof(App)" AdditionalAssemblies="@lazyLoadedAssemblies" OnNavigateAsync="NavigateHandler">
...
</Router>

@code {
  private List<Assembly> lazyLoadedAssemblies = new List<Assembly>();

  private async Task NavigateHandler(NavigationContext args) {
    if (args.EndsWith("TheOneAndOnly") {
        var assemblies = await lazyLoader.LoadAssembliesAsync(new List<string>() { "MyPackage.dll" });
        lazyLoadedAssemblies.AddRange(assemblies);
    }
  }
}
```

**Note:** The lazy-loaded assemblies are passed back to `AdditionalAssemblies` in the event that the assemblies contain routeable components. In that case, we search the new set of assemblies for routes and update our routeable. This enables scenarios where users want to lazy-loaded a collection of pages onto their app.

While lazy-loading, the user might want to showcase a UI to their customer to indicate that a page transition is happening. This PR introduces support for a `Navigating` render fragment that is displayed when the `OnNavigate` async event is running.

```
<Router Assembly="typeof(App)" AdditionalAssemblies="@lazyLoadedAssemblies" OnNavigateAsync="NavigateHandler">
  <Navigating>
    Hang tight, we're bringing you a fancy new page...
  </Navigating>
</Router>
```

In summary, this PR introduces a few changes to support lazy-loading that include:
* Support for a LazyAssemblyLoader service
* API changes to the `Router` to enable lazy-loading
